Subject: Post-demo: infrastructure evaluation & SLA / reserved capacity asks

Alex — thanks again for the demo time today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment on the competitive eval you mentioned versus hyperscaler offerings.

Key takeaways from our call:
- MedLytics wants a direct apples-to-apples on dedicated Redwood pools vs hyperscaler reserved/RI paths (throughput, p95 token latency, cold-start behavior, and cost per 1M tokens).
- Decision drivers: guaranteed capacity during peak batch windows, deterministic tail latency for synchronous workflows, and predictable unit economics for ROI modeling.
- Procurement will need draft SLA language and a pricing anchor for reserved capacity + burst allowance.

Proposed evaluation tests (short form):
1) Baseline steady-state: 1 model, sustained 400 rps for 60m, 512-token average payloads, measure p50/p95/p99 and token efficiency.
2) Burst / concurrency: 5x bursts for 2m every 15m with parallel sessions to test autoscale and pre-warm/cold-start behavior.
3) Failure/fallback: simulate node outage and validate automatic routing to hosted variants and request-level retries.
4) Quantization impact: run same model in FP16 vs 4-bit quant to measure latency and quality delta on your eval prompts.

I've attached a lightweight test matrix (redwood-infra-test-matrix.csv) with fields we need from your side (sample payloads, expected concurrency windows, and a prioritized prompt set). Can you: 1) confirm procurement contact, 2) provide a 2–3 representative payloads (anonymized), and 3) confirm a 4–5 day test window you prefer in early Sep?

Next internal steps on our side: Karthik will scope reserved pool sizing and an SLA draft; Marissa will pull together pricing anchors and drafting for procurement.

Thanks — Sofia

Alex — looping in a few specifics so procurement/infra have the language they need. High level answers then a proposed acceptance-test checklist we can sign off on after you approve the test window 09/06–09/10.

Short answers to your infra bullets:
- SLA type: For Redwood Dedicated (reserved pools) we typically offer an availability SLA on reserved capacity (example: 99.9% uptime for the reserved pool). Latency SLOs at the p95 level are productized as part of an acceptance test for reserved deployments — we can commit to target latency bounds for the agreed test workload and bake that into the acceptance criteria for the reserved pool. In practice, strict p95 latency guarantees are scoped to the workload profile (payload size, batching) rather than a single global figure.
- Hardware pinning: We can prioritize A100-class hardware for a reserved pool in the US region but final mapping depends on the private cluster footprint and lead time; we will document the GPU SKU in the commitment language.
- Burst behavior: Reserved pools include a configurable burst allowance; beyond that, automatic routing to Redwood Hosted (compatible model variant) is enabled as a fallback. We can include a guaranteed burst cushion in the reservation if procurement prefers (example: +30% bursts subject to a surcharge).

Proposed acceptance test checklist (what we will measure during Sep 6–10 run):
1) Throughput verification: sustained 400 rps for 60m, measure token/sec and cost per token.
2) Tail latency: p50/p95/p99 samples for the prioritized prompt set; acceptance criteria = p95 <= agreed target for reserved pool (to be filled once we have sample payloads).
3) Cold-start/resilience: kill one serving node and verify fallback route within 30s, error rate <1% during failover window.
4) Concurrency and burst: trigger 5x bursts and confirm reserved pool scales or falls back to hosted with no more than 2x increase in p95 compared to baseline.
5) Quality regression check: run 200 prompts across FP16 and 4-bit quant variants; acceptable response delta threshold = internal QA pass (we will provide rubric).

Deliverables we will provide by EOD Tue: draft SLA summary, MSA redline (MSA-draft-redwood.pdf), and the populated test matrix with example metrics. Can procurement confirm a 2-month reservation as the pricing anchor for your internal comparison? If yes, Marissa will provide the anchor rates and an example invoice.

If this all looks good I will put the acceptance criteria into a short one-page sign-off (so procurement has something to attach to the MSA).

— Karthik
